The final carry component estimates **loss within one second, conditional on carrying**. It uses a physics-informed competing-risk likelihood with a shared survival probability, logistic arrival gates, and an additive tackle rate. It is separate from end-of-possession xLoss. **own derivation**

## Cohort and evaluation

The cohort contains **9,148 carry attempts, 476 losses (5.20%), across ten SkillCorner matches**. Goalkeeper carriers, shot-ending individual possessions and successful tails shorter than one second are excluded. Goalkeepers remain among defenders. Only the final failed section is a loss; early and zero-duration failures retain the one-second Bernoulli target. Failed passes are outside this task. This training cohort differs from the additional snapshots available for arbitrary-frame evaluation. **design choice**

Five outer folds hold out two complete matches each. Spline transformations and smoothing selection use training matches and inner validation matches; the table pools the five held-out prediction sets. The null model uses each outer training set's loss frequency. Gain is `1 − CE_model / CE_null`; ECE uses ten equal-count quantile bins weighted by their observation counts. CE uses natural logarithms and a probability floor of 1e-6. No resampling or post-hoc calibration is used in the final model. These ten matches also informed model-family development: this is a development benchmark, without an untouched external evaluation. **design choice**

## Log-linear proportional-hazard-inspired model and splines

The starting model uses $\lambda(t)=\lambda_0\exp(\beta_v v_B+\beta_B B(t))$. The additive version replaces the linear covariate shapes with penalized splines; it preserves positive multiplicative rates, defender reachability and shared survival. Both are likelihood-based. This comparison examines functional form, not a standalone Cox proportional-hazards test. See the [ball-drive vignette](vignettes/01_ball_drive_risk/01_ball_drive_risk.ipynb) for equations, references and tracking-based kinematic justification.


| Model | Cross-entropy | Gain over null | Quantile ECE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Log-linear baseline**; historical TTI; Euler | **0.158336** | **22.609%** | **0.902%** |
| Additive speed/boundary reference; historical TTI; Euler | 0.156796 | 23.361% | 0.614% |
| Preserve defender initial speed above the cap | 0.156568 | 23.473% | 0.621% |
| Add individual interception-angle spline | 0.155175 | 24.154% | 0.697% |
| Use signed boundary distance | 0.153320 | 25.060% | 0.644% |
| **Final: exponential Euler, refitted** | **0.153312** | **25.064%** | **0.642%** |

The final Brier score is **0.041968**, ROC AUC **0.87246**. Mean predicted loss is **5.268%**, versus **5.203%** observed. The angle improves cross-entropy without improving pooled ECE in this comparison. The integration change has negligible predictive effect; exponential Euler is retained for probability-mass preservation. Rows describe successive changes on the same cohort, not isolated causal effects.

Signed boundary distance matters mainly for unusual outside-pitch states: 210 trajectories project outside during the horizon, including 45 already outside at the initial frame. About 80.5% of its cross-entropy improvement comes from those 45 rows. This correction should not be presented as a general improvement on ordinary interior carries. Annotation and synchronization noise remain possible; no labels were changed to obtain these results.

The downloadable [metric table](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/metrics.csv), [calibration bins](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/calibration_deciles.csv) and [source hashes](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/provenance.json) contain aggregate results from the outfield log-linear baseline and audited runs 14–15. The baseline and spline rows use the same 9,148 states, labels and outer match pairs; the final changes are presented separately.

```{python}
#| label: fig-carry-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Pooled held-out calibration of the final model; ten equal-count bins."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

calibration = pd.read_csv("data/benchmarks/ball_drive/calibration_deciles.csv")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
ax.plot([0, .3], [0, .3], "--", color="gray", label="Perfect calibration")
ax.plot(calibration.predicted_loss, calibration.observed_loss, "o-", label="Pooled OOF")
ax.set(xlabel="Predicted loss probability", ylabel="Observed loss frequency",
       xlim=(0, .3), ylim=(0, .3))
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Published ball-drive benchmarks

These are numerical references on different datasets, not a common leaderboard. Gains normalize CE against the corresponding null, which helps interpretation but does not remove differences in labels, prevalence, features and splits.

| Study / model | Training loss share | CE | Null CE | Gain over null | Quantile ECE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Fernández et al.; neural network | 9.4% overall | 0.2803 | ≈0.311696* | ≈10.07%* | 0.51% |
| Stalpaert; CatBoost start-only, natural | 6.1% table heading | 0.2059 | 0.2455 | 16.13% | — |
| Stalpaert; CatBoost start-only, resampled | **10% training only** | **0.1053** | 0.2455 | **57.11%** | **1.64%** |
| PRESS; log-linear rate | 5.20% pooled | 0.158336 | 0.204591 | 22.61% | 0.90% |
| PRESS; final additive spline rate | 5.20% pooled | 0.153312 | 0.204591 | 25.06% | 0.64% |

Fernández: Tables 3–4 and §§5.2/6.3–6.6; split by match, 633 matches, one-second sections [@fernandez2021]. *The approximate null is entropy at the published **overall** success rate of 90.6%, not a recovered test-fold null. No pass-risk numbers are mixed into this table.

Stalpaert: Tables 4.4/4.7, §§4.4/4.7; test ratios remain natural. The 1.64% ECE belongs to the selected resampled start-only component, not every row. The prose says 6.3% failed sections, while the natural-training heading says 93.9% success; preserve this discrepancy. He labels the **last two seconds** of failed drives negative; PRESS labels only the terminal section [@stalpaert2022]. Brier scores are 0.0571 (natural) and 0.0251 (10% loss). Values and locators are downloadable in the [comparison table](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/literature_comparison.csv).

### Extension motivated by the 10% resampling result

The large within-study CatBoost gain motivates a different architecture: use a cross-fitted physics prediction plus 2D/context features, then compare natural training with 10% loss training at fixed match folds. Tree splits can express nonlinear interactions and subgroups absent from the present additive rate. Resampling changes their training emphasis; it does not create information. Evaluate on natural held-out data and fit any calibration inside training/validation only. This is an extension to test, not an already established gain for PRESS. **design choice**

The present likelihood's sampling experiments showed no convincing held-out gain after accounting for the changed class prior; raw resampling distorted calibration. Published CatBoost + sampling results therefore motivate this combination rather than replacing the TTI with a more agile routine. The sources do not isolate architecture, features and sampling across datasets. **design choice**

## Closed model specification

The carrier is a point moving as $x_B(t)=x_B(0)+v_B(0)t$. The defender routine retains the historical fixed-position turning delay $v\theta/a_{turn}$, followed by straight-line acceleration toward the target. Maximum linear and turning accelerations are separate user parameters; the benchmark sets both to **7 m/s²**, with **vmax = 7 m/s**. Initial speed above vmax is retained without additional acceleration. The engagement-disc experiment is not included. The runtime does not take an observed acceleration input or use future observed acceleration.

At every integration step, the signed boundary margin is the minimum inward distance to the four lines of a centred **105 × 68 m** pitch. It becomes negative outside; the carrier is neither stopped nor assigned an automatic loss. The log tackle rate combines a baseline, additive speed and boundary effects, and a small individual angle spline. The angle is between carrier velocity and the defender's predicted final approach to the projected carrier position. It is a motion-based heading proxy, not observed posture. Its contribution is masked for carrier speed below 1 m/s or undefined direction. **own derivation**

Speed and boundary use five-knot restricted cubic bases; angle uses four knots. There are no interactions between these effects. The selected smoothing setting was `main_1_angle_100` in all five outer fits. Exponential Euler uses dt = 0.04 s and shares remaining survival mass across defenders. It is first-order for time-varying rates; mass preservation does not establish timestep convergence. The final refit estimates all coefficients and basis transformations anew on the ten matches; fold coefficients are not averaged.

## Use the fitted model on a pitch

This executable example uses **synthetic tracking**, with the verified full-data model bundled in the package. The pitch is illustrative; it contributes no benchmark observations.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fitted-drive-pitch
#| fig-cap: "Synthetic frame evaluated by the final fitted model, using the package's pitch visualization."
from PRESS import PRESS
from PRESS.datasets import load_demo_match
from PRESS.model import BallDriveModel
from PRESS.visualization.plot import plot_pi

tracking, possessions, actions, _ = load_demo_match()
model = BallDriveModel.pretrained()
press = PRESS(tracking, possessions_data=possessions,
              actions_data=actions, ball_drive_model=model)
frame_id = int(press.get_frames(valid_only=True).frame.iloc[0])
press.compute_ball_drive_loss(frame_id, t_press=1.0)
result = press.get_ball_drive_result(frame_id)
print("Model:", result["params"]["model_id"])
print("One-second carry-loss probability:",
      round(float(result["Ball drive loss probability"]), 4))
plot_pi(press, frame_id)
plt.show()
```

`BallDriveModel.from_json(path)` also loads an exported model. `model.predict(...)` evaluates arrays directly, including shorter horizons. Initialization performs no fit. The fitted path is selected explicitly; omitting `ball_drive_model` retains the legacy log-linear API. Short-horizon outputs are supported by integration, but independent calibration at those horizons has not been established. See the [function reference](api.qmd).

## Final refit and checks

Run 16 fits the fixed final specification once on all ten matches. It is **not another test fold** and produces no replacement for the OOF metrics above. Its arrival dispersion is **s = 0.352790** and baseline tackle rate **lambda0 = 0.334747 s⁻¹**; lambda0 is an intercept parameter, not an average tackle probability.

The archive records successful convergence, independently recomputed objective/gradient, positive Hessian and matching covariance. Loading the exported JSON through the frozen package reproduces all 9,148 training predictions within **2.91 × 10⁻⁸** absolute probability; maximum survival-plus-cause mass error is **2.22 × 10⁻¹⁶**. Short horizons 0, 0.17, 0.4 and 1 s are monotone in the verification sample. [Refit provenance](docs/ball-drive-refit-provenance.json).

## Limits and extensions

The model represents average player skills and individual reachability, with limited encounter geometry. Successful and failed carries overlap substantially in available 2D features; this does not prove that all useful 2D information has been exhausted. Body orientation, ball control, contact mechanics, individual ability, annotation error and intrinsic outcome variation can contribute. Collective defensive behaviour and richer tactical context remain extensions. Tracking velocities use a centred seven-frame window: this offline benchmark is not a strictly causal live system.

A more flexible tree model with contextual features, the physics likelihood as an input and training-only resampling is a separate future architecture. The resampling experiments on the present likelihood did not show a convincing held-out benefit. Published numbers above are contextual benchmarks with their definitions and sampling differences recorded, not a same-dataset ranking.

## Pass risk: historical curvature diagnostic

Before fitting the pass-control parameters, the archived raw/Platt results have been reproduced. They use one five-match calibration / five-match test split. The held-out match identities are the same in both rows; curvature filtering changes the passes and their loss prevalence, and Platt is refitted on each corresponding training cohort. These are historical diagnostics, separate from the new five-fold benchmark under preparation.

| Historical cohort | Test passes | Observed loss | Raw CE | Platt CE | Platt quantile ECE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| All available scored passes | 3,683 | 15.48% | 0.202532 | 0.173942 | 1.441% |
| Curvature <10% | 2,768 | 12.83% | 0.162329 | 0.135552 | 0.752% |

The [reproduced table](data/benchmarks/pass_risk/historical_curvature_comparison.csv) supports reporting better loss and calibration on straighter passes. This is consistent with limitations of a flight model without spin or Magnus effects [@spearman2017], but does not identify spin as the sole cause: selection changes pass difficulty, outcomes and tracking quality. It motivates a separate curvature-stratified diagnostic and later tests of the flight boundary condition. Curvature is measured after the pass and is not used as a predictor available before release. **design choice**

The next comparison keeps one audited outfield-passer cohort and five fixed held-out match pairs: fixed physics with/without training-only Platt, then direct estimation of lambda control and arrival dispersion s without Platt, for vmax **5 and 5.5 m/s**. A numerical integration control separates exponential Euler from parameter calibration. Spin remains unmodeled; no new pass-risk performance is claimed before that run completes.
